newsitem.title: USA: SEC votes to send mutual fund reforms for comment.
newsitem.headline: SEC votes to send mutual fund reforms for comment.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission Thursday proposed long-awaited reforms to make it easier for investors to select from the nation's more than 6,000 mutual funds.
SEC commissioners voted 4-0 to send the proposals out for public scrutiny. A 90-day public comment period follows publication in the Federal Register.
"Today's proposals represent the most sweeping revision of mutual fund disclosure in 14 years," SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt said at the commission's opening meeting.
The proposals respond to investors' concerns and will help them evaluate whether a particular fund is right for them, Levitt said.
The first initative would overhaul prospectus requirements and the registration form for funds, making it easier for investors to use and easier for funds to prepare.

The proposal focuses on essential information about a particular fund, such as investment strategies, risks and fees that investors need to know before investing. Risk disclosure would emphasise the risk of the fund's investments as a whole.

A new risk/return summary at the front of all prospectuses would include a description of the fund's overall risks, a bar chart reflecting the fund's 10-year returns and a table that compares the performance with a broad-based securities market index.
The second rule bans misleading mutual fund names by making them match the investment style and objectives of the fund.
Commissioner Steven Wallman expressed some concern over one component of the names proposal that seeks to prevent the misleading use of the words "government," "guaranteed" or "tax-exempt."
"The confusion we've seen ... evidenced in the past with regard to not understanding how a bond fund works isn't dependent on the name," Wallman said.

"Merely making the name different ... I don't think avoids that confusion," he said. "Many people invest in (government-backed) funds with the expectation that it was like a savings account ... but they thought the principal was safe," he said.
Concerns raised will not be resolved by simply banning the use of "guaranteed" in connection with the use of the words U.S. government, Wallman said.
The confusion arises whether it is "U.S. government guaranteed securities" or just "U.S. government securities," which is currently allowed, or "U.S. Treasuries," or things of that nature, he said.
"It's the lack of understanding how bond funds work as compared to the notion of what's in a name that's causing some confusion," Wallman said after the meeting.

The initiative also would require a fund with a name suggesting that it focuses on a particular type of investment to invest at least 80 percent of its assets accordingly, up from the current 65 percent.

The final initiative would permit a fund to provide investors with a fund profile summarizing key fund information, including investment strategies, risks, performances and fees in a concise standardised format.
The profile includes information on the fund's investment adviser and portfolio manager, purchase and redemption procedures, tax implications and shareholder services.
